t: Maximum Subarray Sum with One Deletion — Editorial
o: We must pick a contiguous subarray and may delete at most one element from it (the result must stay non-empty), maximizing the remaining sum. In Example 1, taking the whole array [1,-2,0,3] and deleting -2 gives 4. In Example 2, deleting anything never beats just taking [3], so the answer is 3. Example 3 shows we cannot delete the only element of a length-1 subarray, so all-negative arrays return their maximum element. With n up to 1e5, an O(n^2) enumeration of subarrays is too slow; we need an O(n) DP that tracks state about whether a deletion has been used.
k: Track two DP states per index: best subarray ending here with no deletion, and best subarray ending here with exactly one deletion.
The one-deletion state can either extend a previous one-deletion state or delete the current element from a no-deletion state ending at the previous index.
Initialize answers with arr[0] to correctly handle all-negative arrays where deletion is not allowed to empty the subarray.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with Prefix/Suffix Max (Kadane precomputation)
a.i: For each element i considered as the deleted one, the answer candidate is (best subarray sum ending at i-1) + (best subarray sum starting at i+1). Precompute forward Kadane (max subarray ending at each index) and backward Kadane (max subarray starting at each index), then combine in O(n). Also consider the plain maximum subarray without any deletion.
s: Compute f[i] = max sum of a subarray ending at i via Kadane: f[i] = max(arr[i], f[i-1] + arr[i]).
Compute g[i] = max sum of a subarray starting at i similarly from the right: g[i] = max(arr[i], g[i+1] + arr[i]).
Answer is max over i of f[i] (no deletion), and for 0 < i < n-1, f[i-1] + g[i+1] (delete arr[i]).
a.t: O(n) — three linear passes over the array.
a.sp: O(n) — two auxiliary arrays f and g.

a.n: Approach 2: One-Pass DP with Two States (Optimal)
a.i: Maintain two rolling values: noDel = best subarray sum ending at current index using zero deletions, and oneDel = best subarray sum ending at current index using exactly one deletion. When processing arr[i]: oneDel becomes max(oneDel + arr[i], noDel_prev) — either extend the previous one-deletion subarray, or delete arr[i] itself by inheriting the previous no-deletion value. noDel is standard Kadane. The answer is the max of all states seen, initialized to arr[0]. This is equivalent to Approach 1 but uses O(1) space and handles edges naturally.
s: For each i from 1 to n-1: oneDel = max(oneDel + arr[i], noDel); then noDel = max(noDel + arr[i], arr[i]) (update order matters — use old noDel for oneDel).
Update ans = max(ans, noDel, oneDel) after each step.
a.t: O(n) — single pass with constant work per element.
a.sp: O(1) — only three scalar variables beyond the input.

w: In an interview, present the brute-force idea briefly (delete each element, combine left/right Kadane results) to show understanding, then implement the O(1)-space two-state DP as it is cleaner and faster. Common pitfalls: forgetting that a length-1 subarray cannot be emptied (so all-negative inputs return the max element, not 0); updating noDel before oneDel in the same iteration (which would wrongly allow deleting the current element twice); and initializing the answer to 0 instead of arr[0]. Edge cases: single-element arrays, all negatives, and arrays where the optimal move is no deletion at all. Follow-ups might ask for k deletions (generalize to a DP array indexed by number of deletions used) or returning the actual subarray indices (store parent pointers/argmax positions alongside the DP values).
